 WILLIAMSON COUNTIES

              REPLY BRIEF OF INTERVENORS THE MOSELEY GROUP
                 AND MULTIPLE FORMER PRO SE INTERVENORS

       Intervenors James Gregory Waller, Marilyn Moseley Waller, Arthur Kyle Moseley, David

Moseley (Moseley Group), W. Trent & Deanna Lea Barley, AH (“Bert”) Broad III, Stephen T.

Broad, Christina Broad Ramsey, Kolt Bunch, Dahlberg Estate – Alice Powell, Dahlberg Estate –

Carol Pilgrim, Trustee, Jordan Moore & Dalke Investments, LP, M. Rex & Kellie A. Emerson,

Micheal Gibbs, Joe Johanson, Mark & Regina Kyzer, Lundgren, Carlton/Carlton &

Marilyn/Marilyn-Robert Kreig Trust, Matt & Suzzette McBee, Archie Morris, R.A. Morris, T.K.

Morris, Brant Myers (leases from Bonnie Brotherton) Wanye-Kenneth Nowlin, Joe Don Pace;

Donna Phillips, Joanna Kaye Schackelford, Sharry Ware, John & Cheri Warriner, and Jared

Whitworth (leases from Teresa Weber) submit this Reply Brief. These parties will at times be

called the “Multiple Intervenors” in this Reply Brief.

       This Reply Brief specifically responds to assertions made in the Initial Briefs of the Brady

Creek Intervenors, the Solana Intervenors, and 4K Land & Cattle. These intervenors advocate for

Route 392, which includes Link U3 crossing the Colorado River. The evidence shows that U3


                                                 1
 presents significant negatives and does not justify Route 392’s higher cost or increased habitable

structures.

                       REPLY TO THE BRADY CREEK INTERVENORS

        Page 3 (Role of Applicants and PUC Staff): The ALJs and the Commissioners should

consider that the group of experts not being paid by any intervenor, those of Applicants and Mr.

Poole, gave the most objective testimony. The work of these nonpartisan experts is compelling.

Applicants identified six final routes for the most detailed analysis; none contain Link U31. Mr.

Poole identified Route 487 as best meeting the criteria2; it does not contain U3. Moreover, all seven

of these routes contain Links K13-K51-K52-M113, which the big landowners and their hired

experts opposed.

        Pages 7 and 25 (J22 Crossing): J22 does not parallel an existing transmission line, but it

complies with the specific recommendations of the Texas Parks & Wildlife Department (TPWD)

for crossing streams. TPWD said transmission lines should be “crossing streams in a perpendicular

manner and avoiding placement of lines parallel to streams and their associated wooded

corridors4.” As shown from the admitted exhibits below5, J22 will cross in a perpendicular manner

and not run parallel to the Colorado River. In sharp contrast6, U3’s crossing is not perpendicular

and U3 runs parallel to the Colorado River for almost two miles.

            Page 10 (Expertise of Those Opposed to U3): Characterizing experts as opposed or

unopposed to a specific link does not accurately portray the evidence. As explained above, Mr.

Poole identified Route 487 as best meeting PUC criteria; Applicants identified six final routes, of

which they identified Route 894 as best meeting PUC criteria. None of these seven routes use Link

U3. Moreover, several other intervenors’ experts identified a route with a crossing other than U3

as best satisfying PUC criteria, including Aaron Brewer, Brian Andrews, Jason Buntz, and Ryan

Hopkins.

           Page 10-11 (No Expert Consensus on U3): As explained above, no “expert consensus”

advocated for U3. Mr. Poole, with over ten years’ experience as a PUC engineer, recognized the

reliability concerns posed by U3. He testified that U3’s proximity to an existing transmission line

in an area of high-intensity convective thunderstorms elevates the risk of simultaneous outages7.

           Page 18 and generally in all three Initial Briefs (Impacts to Specific Intervenors):

Multiple pages in each of these Initial Briefs suggest that the effect of a transmission line on their

land is especially devastating. They suggest that a transmission line on their large landholdings

does more damage than would the same line crossing multiple smaller ranches. No evidence

supports this suggestion. While property-specific testimony may illuminate the routing criteria,

generalized claims of uniquely severe harm cannot substitute for a route-wide comparison using

the PUC criteria.

           Page 19 (Criticism of General Cost Analysis): Consideration of cost is an important

factor in this case and in virtually every routing case. Criticism of Applicants’ cost estimation

analysis does not and should not remove cost as a factor. The Commissioners have considered

cost, evaluated with the same basic approach as Applicants have used in this case, for as long as



7
    Transcript, Day 3 (Poole) at 220:10-221:2; See also M31 Ex. 9 (McAdams Cross Rebuttal) at 13:9-15

                                                         4
 PUC has been conducting route selections. Asking the ALJs and the Commissioners to disregard

the cost analysis, which shows Route 392 costing far more than 487 or 894, is a request to ignore

longstanding PUC policy, PUC regulations, and PURA.

         Pages 20-21 (Criticism of Cost Analysis Process): In their cost estimating, Applicants

used a rigorous and tested methodology. As the Supreme Court of Texas observed, “We think it

unwise to depart from the methodology that is at present generally accepted.” Merrell Dow

Pharmaceuticals v. Havner, 953 S.W.2d 706, 724 (Tex. 1997)

         Applicants then spent months developing and refining the methodology to the specific

circumstances in this case8. The process allowed Applicants to make an additional confirmation of

the validity of their methodology by comparing their individual cost models and determining that

the “estimates aligned extremely well9.” With the estimates aligning so well, “Applicants agreed

to proceed with a unified cost approach that utilized Oncor’s cost model in combination with each

respective utility’s spotting procedures and contingency percentages for their respective portions

of the line10.” In summary, “This approach ensured consistency in structure spotting across all

links and, therefore, uniformity in estimating all links, which, in turn, created accurate

differentiation between routes to best inform the Commission in selecting the final route11.”

         Assertions that Applicants do not understand how the terrain differences can affect cost are

contradicted by the evidence: “Applicants’ respective construction practices have been

successfully used across Texas in areas with varying terrain and geologic features to establish

stable foundations that support its transmission structures12.” As shown in the specific discussion

cost estimating methodology to the specific information for each link13.

           Applicants’ cost analysis is consistent with evidence in the case regarding terrain. Far from

showing Applicants failed to account for terrain differences, their analysis accounted for the

challenges in the western portion of the study area. In cost per mile, Route 410 is slightly less than

392 ($7.440 million and $7.488 million respectively). Both 392 and 410 have a lower cost per mile

than 894 and 487 ($7.532 million and $7.516 million respectively). The similarity of the routes up

to G51 and the Applicants’ higher cost estimates for 392 and 410 demonstrate that Applicants’

analysis identified a slight increase in cost per mile in the western routes that use K13-K51-K52-

M11.

           No witness testified that they had calculated a higher increase in cost for the western routes

than that shown in Applicants’ cost analysis.

           Importantly, the slightly higher cost per mile of Routes 392 and 410 does not justify

selecting either of those routes over Routes 894 or 487. Project cost is of course a function of both

rate and distance. Compared to Routes 894 and 487, Routes 392 and 410 are 6-12 miles longer,

and therefore cost up to $67 million more, and directly affect up to 51 more habitable

structures. While Applicants appear to agree that the cost per mile of using K13-K51-K52-M11

will be slightly higher than other options, Applicants, the PUC Staff, and multiple experts reject

the notion that slightly higher costs per mile along K13-K51-K52-M11 prevent 894 or 487 from

best meeting the PUC criteria, overall .




13
     Applicants’ Ex. 9 (Elliott Reb.) at 18:1-21

         Page 28 (Tower Construction): Applicants are well aware of the potential presence of a

cave, karst, or cistern. Their first approach is to go over14; or to go around15. Further, “If avoidance

is not feasible, Applicants would employ practices focused on minimizing and remediating

potential impacts16.” Applicants have multiple tools to ensure safe and effective tower

construction17. These tools and their experience are extensive, “By utilizing engineering expertise,

maintaining strict sediment controls, and cooperating with the landowner, the impacts can be

effectively managed and minimized 18.”

        Pages 28-32 (Value of Dr. Turnbough’s Opinion): Dr. Turnbough characterized the

difference in habitable structures between Route 392 and Route 894 (a difference of 51 structures

over 225 miles) as numerically insignificant19. Just three weeks before, he called a difference of

105 structures over 365 miles (140 miles longer) a “large disparity20.” When asked about how he

can characterize one as “numerically insignificant” and another as “large disparity,” he admitted:

“There is no standard21.”

        Page 32 (U3 Crossing the Colorado River): The experts for these intervenors ignore the

many negatives caused by U3. Route 894, which uses Link J22 to cross the Colorado River, does

not have these negatives. U3 crosses at an ecologically significant stream segment (ESSS)22; Link

J22 does not23. U3 crosses at USFWS critical habitat24; J22 does not25. For approximately two

         Pages 36 and 43 (Terrain Suitability): Applicants provided ample evidence of their

near Links K13-K51-K52-M11. The evidence indicates the terrain near Links K13-K51-K52-M11

will have some challenges, which Applicants are more than qualified to meet. Those challenges

did not prevent the PUC Staff from recommending a route containing Links K13-K51-K52-M11,

nor did they prevent Applicants from identifying all six of their final candidate routes as containing

Links K13-K51-K52-M11.

                              REPLY TO THE SOLANA INTERVENORS

         Pages 3-8 (Colorado River Crossing): As explained above, experts for the Solana and

Brady Creek Intervenors ignored multiple negative attributes of crossing the Colorado River at

Link U3. Perhaps most notably, none of the experts addressed the risks of having the transmission

occurs during high-intensity convective thunderstorms35. Dr. Sansom admitted he was unaware of

this attribute of the North-Central Prairies MLRA36. None of the other “experts” advocating U3

indicated they were aware; none of them addressed the issue.

         Pages 6-7 (J22 Crossing): As explained above, J22 follows TPWD recommendations.

J22’s crossing is perpendicular; U3’s is not. J22 avoids paralleling the Colorado River; U3 parallels

the Colorado River for almost two miles.

         Pages 10-13 (Future Development): The evidence demonstrates that the “development”

cited by the Solana Intervenors is too speculative to be given much weight. In their Initial Brief,

the Solana Intervenors acknowledged: development financing remains pending (“development

financing is in its final stages37”) and the developer’s investment is largely to come (“DMB and

its partners have committed approximately $10 million in pre-development investment38”). The

testimony of DMB’s representative is also clear that little no observable work has been done. At

most, DMB has done some “initial clearing and cleanup activities in portions of the Ranch.39”

While the project requires “significant roadway infrastructure,” the project has only completed

negotiations, as “[d]etails of that infrastructure have been negotiated with the Counties40.”

Similarly, “Rights of way have been negotiated with two surrounding owners41.” Financing is not

final; “projections and analyses are part of the ongoing work necessary to finance and implement

a development of this scale42.” The evidence showed incomplete financing; little physical work;

        Applicants used PUC criteria and generally accepted methodology. They properly did not

give much weight to contracts with municipal utility districts to provide future service, wastewater

discharge permit applications, preliminary plats, contracts with civil engineering firms, or other

aspects of future development.

                                   REPLY TO 4K LAND & CATTLE

        Pages 8-14 (Route Development): Applicants used PUC criteria and accepted

methodology in their route development. In addition to extensive community outreach, the

identification and analysis of individual routes and links was extensive. Applicants initially

identified 1,246 alternative routes; they narrowed those to 122 alternative routes44 and then to 30

routes45 and finally to six46. The fact that all six final routes, and the route identified by the PUC

Staff (487), all include K13-K51-K52-M11 and none of them use U3 does not mean the route

development was flawed. Rather, extensive analysis has demonstrated that Link U3 and Route 392

significantly underperform Routes 894 and 487 on the PUC criteria.

        These Intervenors fail to understand the fundamental approach to route analysis. Routing

decisions are inherently “judgment calls,” requiring the balancing of often competing goals that

may be more or less important in any specific case. Dunn v. Public Util. Comm’n, 246 S.W.3d

788, 795 (Tex. App.-Austin 2008, no pet.)

        Labelling the methodology a “black box” or other criticisms of Applicants route

development do not establish failure to follow PUC regulations and criteria. Mr. Scott’s “six

elements” are not in the Texas Administrative Code, nor do the Solana Intervenors cite a single

 regulation or PUC policy not followed by Applicants in their route development.

           Page 16 (TPWD Recommendations): Those advocating for U3 are the ones who are

disregarding the input of TPWD. While TPWD made a general recommendation for “routing new

transmission and distribution lines along existing roads, pipelines, transmission lines, or other

utility rights-of way (ROW)…47,” TPWD made specific recommendations for stream crossings.

TPWD transmission lines should be “crossing streams in a perpendicular manner and avoiding

placement of lines parallel to streams and their associated wooded corridors48.” Link U3 disregards

specific TPWD recommendations at one of the most important crossings this line will make.

           Applicants did not need to make any changes based on TPWD’s recommendations.

Applicants wisely appreciated that the specific outweighs the general. They followed TPWD’s

specific recommendations when they determined routes not using Link U3 best met PUC criteria,

including the PUC requirement to consider TPWD’s input.

           Pages 18-22 (Specific Impact to 4K): As discussed above, every intervenor claims a

transmission line will have a unique impact on their land. 4K does not get special treatment because

its lawyer uses multiple pages to describe those impacts. While property-specific testimony may

illuminate the routing criteria, generalized claims of uniquely severe harm cannot substitute for a

route-wide comparison using the PUC criteria.

                                           CONCLUSION

           The Initial Briefs of the Brady Creek Intervenors, the Solana Intervenors, and 4K Land &

Cattle are unpersuasive. Applicants and the PUC Staff agree that the route that best meets PUC

criteria will contain Links K13-K51-K52-M1; it will not contain Link U3.
